instantiated_cells.justification: “Lobbying” is defined as attempting to influence legislative or administrative action by oral or written communication, including appearances at public hearings or meetings (events) and preparation time.

The definition of “lobbyist” turns on being an individual employed by or receiving economic consideration from a principal and making lobbying communications, and does not enumerate specific actor types like law firms or consultancies.
The provided definitions section does not define the term “public entity.”

Coverage turns on quantitative thresholds (e.g., principal registers after exceeding $500/year; verified statement exemption if ≤$500/year; an individual is a lobbyist only if lobbying communications occur on at least 5 days in a reporting period when duties are not exclusively lobbying).
Lobbying includes communications with elective state officials and legislative employees and seeks to influence “legislative action,” which expressly includes the governor’s approval/veto actions.
Lobbying/lobbying communications target elective state officials, agency officials, and legislative employees, covering both legislative and executive/administrative branch officials and staff.

The statutory definition of lobbying covers attempts to influence legislative action via communications with elective state officials and legislative employees, and legislative action includes the governor’s approval or veto.
Lobbying is defined to include communications attempting to influence legislative action, and legislative action expressly includes action of the governor (executive) in approving or vetoing bills.

Lobbying includes attempts to influence administrative action via communications with agency officials (executive agencies) and legislative action via communications with elective state officials including the governor.

Targets of lobbying communications are elective state officials, agency officials, and legislative employees, encompassing the legislative branch and executive/administrative officials and their staff.

Elective state officials, local officials, tribal officials, and legislative employees are generally not subject to lobbying regulation provisions when acting in an official capacity, rather than being required to register.

Agency employees paid a salary whose regular duties include attempting to influence legislative action are reported by agencies under §13.695, and the lobbyist definition includes compensation/time standards (economic consideration; 5 days in a reporting period when not exclusively lobbying).
The definitions of “agency” and “principal” are not based on public charter or special government protection as a criterion for coverage.
Neither the “lobbyist” nor “principal” definitions rely on ownership characteristics; they rely on employment/compensation relationships and lobbying activity.
The statutory definitions do not classify covered entities by structure or composition of revenue, but instead by organizational form and lobbying employment/compensation arrangements.
